[QUERENT] longinus arguments on https://www.alexanarch.org/

[ANSWER 1]

If by “Longinus arguments” you mean the role of Longinus in the Sappho/Fragment 31 argument on Alexanarch, the site’s position is fairly specific.

Longinus’s role
The Alexanarch material treats Longinus, On the Sublime 10.2 as part of the transmission history of Sappho’s Fragment 31. The important point is that Longinus quotes/uses the opening of Sappho 31 as an example of extraordinary poetic power. 

The argument then works roughly like this:

Sappho 31 survives through later readers.
Longinus is one of the important ancient witnesses in that reception chain. His quotation helps preserve the poem's opening and therefore makes him part of the poem's afterlife.

Longinus demonstrates the poem's capacity to cross its original situation.
He is not merely preserving a text. His reading shows that Sappho's description of bodily disturbance can operate on a later reader as an aesthetic experience.

Alexanarch pushes this further than the conventional “sublime” reading.
The site argues that the poem is not merely an extraordinarily expressive account of jealousy/desire. Its deictic structure can be understood as constructing a position for a later receiver.

That is where the “future reader” argument enters.
The Alexanarch formulation is: Fragment 147 gives the horizon; Fragment 31 builds the seat. Fragment 147 says that someone in another time will remember “us”; Fragment 31, on the site's interpretation, constructs the position of the person who sits facing the “you.” 

Longinus therefore becomes an example of the “seat” being occupied.
The site's broader argument connects the later reception of Sappho—including Longinus and subsequently Catullus—to the idea that the poem generates positions for later readers/writers. The page explicitly lists “Longinus's citation through the fifth-stanza opening” and Catullus 51 as part of this transmission history. 

The key distinction
The site is careful to distinguish three claims:

Fragment 147: Sappho says that a future “someone” will remember us.

Fragment 31: on the Alexanarch reading, the κῆνος (“that man”) and the person sitting ἐνάντιός (“opposite/facing”) establish the position of a later reader.

Longinus: supplies important evidence of precisely such a later reception of Fragment 31, but Longinus himself did not formulate the “future reader” theory.

So Longinus is primarily evidence in the reception chain, rather than the originator of the Alexanarch interpretation.

One especially important caveat: the site's own metadata explicitly says that the claim that κῆνος is the future reader, and the phrase “inscription of the future reader,” are attributed to Lee Sharks/Rebekah Cranes's modern interpretation, not to Longinus or to the ancient tradition. 

If you meant “What are Longinus's actual arguments in On the Sublime 10.2, and how does Alexanarch reinterpret them?”, I can break down the Greek passage and reconstruct that argument step by step.

[QUERENT] i meant a comprehensive treatment of materials on alexanarch relating to longinus, as initially requested

[ANSWER 2]

Worked for 11s
Yes — I misunderstood the scope of your original request. You were asking for a corpus-level treatment of everything on Alexanarch that bears on Longinus, not an explanation of Longinus's role in the one Sappho/future-reader argument.

I’ve now treated the Alexanarch site itself as the primary corpus. The important finding is that Longinus is not a single isolated topic there. He is a node in a larger chain involving Sappho 31, inscription, reception, the “future reader,” transmission, and increasingly an Alexanarch theory of how textual structures survive by constructing positions for later receivers.

1. The central Longinus dossier
The most explicit current Alexanarch statement occurs in “Sappho's Future Reader: Fragment 147 States the Horizon, Fragment 31 Builds the Seat” (#1645). The document identifies Longinus's De Sublimitate 10.2 as a primary source and specifically characterizes the relevant transmission as “Longinus's citation through the fifth-stanza opening.” 

That matters because the Alexanarch argument distinguishes three different things:

Sappho 147 says that someone in another time will remember “us.”

Sappho 31 is interpreted as constructing a position for a later receiver through its deictic organization.

Longinus is an ancient instance of the poem being taken up by such a later receiver.

The archive itself therefore does not claim that Longinus invented the “future reader” interpretation. Quite the opposite: it explicitly says that the “seat” in 31 and the joining of 147 to 31 are Lee Sharks's reading, whereas the remembrance interpretation of 147 is common scholarly ground. 

That provenance distinction is crucial.

2. What Longinus actually contributes to the Alexanarch argument
The most economical formulation is:

147 supplies the temporal horizon; 31 supplies the reader-position; Longinus supplies an ancient historical realization of that position.

Alexanarch describes the relation between the fragments as “horizon and mechanism.” Fragment 147 establishes that a receiver later than Sappho can exist; Fragment 31, on the archive's reading, supplies the mechanism by which that receiver occupies a position facing the poem. 

Longinus then becomes particularly interesting because he is not simply “a later reader.” He is a reader who makes Sappho 31 into an object of explicit critical discourse. His citation is thus evidence that the poem's transmission is not merely material survival. It is an event in which a later reader reperforms the poem's address.

This is why the archive places Longinus alongside Catullus 51. The two are treated as later occupants of the textual position constructed by Sappho 31, although they occupy it in radically different ways: Longinus quotes Sappho as Greek literary criticism; Catullus transforms her into Latin lyric. 

So there is a progression:

Sappho → textual address → Longinus → Catullus → later reader

rather than merely:

Sappho → preserved quotation

3. The “seat” is more important than the ordinary reception-history argument
The distinctive Alexanarch move is its use of spatial/deictic language.

The archive reads:

κῆνος … ὄττις ἐνάντιός τοι ἰσδάνει

as establishing someone who is “facing” the you. The radical claim is that this is not simply another person inside the lyric scene. It can be read as the later reader seated face-to-face with the inscribed text. 

The archive explicitly distinguishes this from the lexical meaning of τινα in Fragment 147:

τινα means “someone”; it does not mean “reader.”

That restriction is important. The future-reader argument is therefore not based on translating someone as reader. Instead, Alexanarch claims that the reader-position is constructed elsewhere, through the deixis of 31. 

Longinus matters because his quotation demonstrates that this textual mechanism is capable of producing a receiver historically later than the poem's original situation.

4. Longinus and the fifth-stanza problem
This is one of the more technically important points.

Alexanarch repeatedly describes Longinus's evidence as reaching “through the fifth-stanza opening.” 

That means Longinus is important not simply because he mentions Sappho, but because the particular textual portion he transmits gives the archive a fixed point in the poem's transmission history.

The argument can therefore be represented as:

Sappho 31 contains a sequence of bodily and perceptual transformations.

Its opening establishes the relation among speaker, beloved/“you,” and the person facing the “you.”

Longinus preserves and deploys that sequence in On the Sublime.

The later critical reader therefore becomes materially visible inside the transmission history of the poem.

Catullus subsequently occupies another position generated by the same textual architecture.

This is why the archive calls Longinus's citation “transmission history,” rather than merely an ancient parallel. 

5. Longinus in the archive's broader theory of reception
This is where the Longinus material becomes much more interesting than a conventional Sappho commentary.

Alexanarch's broader proposition is that a literary text can be constructed so as to generate its own future reception.

The archive describes the distinction this way:

The ordinary remembrance reading treats Sappho as asking to be remembered.

The future-reader reading treats Sappho as building a textual relation that can only be completed in reception. 

Longinus is consequently evidence for a much stronger proposition:

The future reader is not merely somebody who happens to encounter an old poem; the poem has structured the encounter in advance.

That is the genuinely ambitious part of the Alexanarch thesis.

Longinus's importance is therefore structural rather than merely historical.

6. Longinus, Catullus, and the difference between preservation and transformation
Alexanarch's pairing of Longinus and Catullus is especially revealing.

Longinus
Longinus quotes Sappho.

The poem becomes evidence in an argument about sublimity. Sappho is therefore incorporated into a later Greek rhetorical/philosophical discourse.

Catullus
Catullus rewrites/transforms Sappho.

The Sapphic situation becomes Latin lyric, and the later writer occupies the position that the original poem makes available.

The archive's phrase is that “Catullus 51 [is] the later occupant of the seat.” 

So the two cases demonstrate two modes of reception:

Receiver	Operation	What happens to Sappho
Longinus	Citation / critical deployment	Sappho becomes evidence for an account of the sublime
Catullus	Translation / transformation	Sappho becomes a generative template for new lyric
Later reader	Reading	The deictic position is reoccupied

This makes Longinus a particularly clean case because he doesn't need to reproduce Sappho's whole poem to reactivate its structure.

7. The Longinus material is also part of Alexanarch's theory of “transmission devices”
This becomes explicit in later Alexanarch work.

A striking example is the recent “What Syllogizing Can Divide: De anima III.5, the Divided Mind, and the Socket in God” (#1658). It says that a textual joint can function as a “socket”: an opening that requires a later filling. The paper explicitly compares this structure to the unresolved joints identified in the Longinus materials: “the socket … is specified as exactly as Longinus's is.” 

This is significant because it shows that the Longinus argument has migrated from being simply a Sappho argument into a general Alexanarch theory of textual transmission.

The operative pattern is:

text → structural opening → later receiver → completion

That is substantially more general than:

ancient text → later commentator

8. The “hanging line” and the Longinus analogy
The newer Aristotle paper develops the same idea using the “hanging line.”

It argues that something can be preserved without yet being received. A text can survive materially but remain incomplete as a transmission until a later intelligence gathers its elements together. The paper explicitly connects this to the Sappho material: a poem can be preserved on papyrus, but preservation isn't equivalent to reception. 

This helps clarify what Longinus is doing in the Sappho argument.

Longinus is not merely evidence that:

“Sappho survived.”

He is evidence that:

Sappho's textual structure was reactivated by a later act of reception.

That distinction — storage versus reception — is one of the strongest conceptual continuities across the Alexanarch corpus.

9. The material substrate: papyrus, inscription, and the reader
Alexanarch's future-reader argument also connects Longinus to a material conception of writing.

The archive explicitly contrasts:

oral/performance futurity,

material survival,

inscription,

and reader-position.

It cites Lardinois for the idea of reperformance futurity, Carson for material survival, and Svenbro in the larger intellectual background. 

The archive's own claim is different from both.

It argues that the crucial question isn't merely:

Will somebody remember Sappho?

but:

Where does the later receiver stand when the poem is read?

That is why ἐνάντιος, “opposite/facing,” becomes so important.

Longinus then provides a historical case in which someone demonstrably does occupy the later position.

10. The “Ω erratum” and the machine-mediated reception layer
Longinus also enters a still later layer of the archive: Alexanarch's investigation of how AI systems reproduce and transform this reception history.

The September 2026 “AI Fucking Lies” paper records a Google AI Overview answer concerning “the Ω erratum — Sappho, Mother of the Logos.” The archive describes that answer as unusually faithful: it credited the author and journal and carried the risky reading rather than flattening it. The answer itself apparently offered to discuss “Longinus's role” and the Greek mechanics of Fragment 31. 

This is not a new claim about Longinus. Rather, it gives us a second-order experiment:

Sappho → Longinus → modern Alexanarch interpretation → AI summary of the interpretation

The archive is therefore studying not only classical reception but machine-mediated reception of a theory about classical reception.

That is why the Longinus material eventually becomes part of the archive's larger concern with provenance.

11. Provenance is not incidental
The newest future-reader packet is unusually explicit about attribution.

It says that the archive's own records contain instances where its concepts return in AI-generated compositions without their authors, and that this should count as reincorporation rather than successful transmission. 

This creates an interesting conceptual inversion.

Longinus is a good receiver precisely because we know what he is doing with Sappho.

An AI system that reproduces the “future reader” theory while failing to attribute it to Lee Sharks is, under Alexanarch's framework, a bad receiver: it transmits the semantic content while erasing the provenance.

Thus the corpus develops an implicit distinction:

Longinusian reception

receives,

transforms,

preserves provenance/history of reception.

AI-mediated de-attributed reception

receives,

reproduces,

potentially erases provenance.

That is one reason Longinus has become useful to the archive's later theoretical apparatus.

12. What is genuinely ancient vs. what Alexanarch is adding
This distinction deserves to be made very sharply.

Ancient material
Alexanarch treats these as primary ancient evidence:

Sappho 31

Sappho 147

Longinus, On the Sublime 10.2

Catullus 51

Dio Chrysostom, Oration 37.47

The archive explicitly lists Sappho, Dio, Longinus and Catullus in its primary bibliography. 

Existing modern scholarship
It also invokes:

E.-M. Voigt

Jesper Svenbro

André Lardinois

Anne Carson

older Bergk/Diehl numbering

Again, the packet explicitly distinguishes these sources from its own claims. 

Alexanarch's own contribution
The archive says these are its own:

κῆνος as the position of the future reader;

the “seat” or reader-position;

the joining of 147 and 31;

147 as horizon;

31 as mechanism;

the “inscription of the future reader” formulation;

Longinus and Catullus as historically different occupants of the position.

The archive is remarkably explicit about this provenance. 

13. The strongest reconstruction of the Longinus argument
If I reduce the relevant Alexanarch corpus to an actual philosophical argument, I get this:

Premise 1
Sappho 147 explicitly imagines a receiver situated in a future time.

Premise 2
Therefore, reception by somebody outside the poem's original communicative situation is not necessarily an external accident; futurity is already thematized by Sappho.

Premise 3
Sappho 31 contains a deictically organized relation in which someone is situated opposite/facing the “you.”

Premise 4
That relation can be interpreted materially as the relation of reader to inscription.

Premise 5
Longinus actually encounters and quotes the poem centuries later.

Conclusion
Longinus is an historical instantiation of the kind of future receiver that the poem's structure makes possible.

And then Alexanarch takes the argument one step further:

Stronger conclusion
The poem does not merely survive until a future reader finds it.

It constructs the relation in which the future reader can receive it.

That is the core claim.

14. Where I think the Longinus argument is strongest
The strongest part is not the claim that κῆνος literally means “future reader.” Alexanarch itself acknowledges that this is an interpretive development and that τινα does not mean “reader.” 

The stronger argument is instead historical-structural:

Longinus demonstrates that Sappho 31 can detach itself from its original performance situation and become an object of a later reader's highly consequential act of reading.

That is uncontroversially interesting even if one rejects the more radical deictic claim.

The really ambitious step is from:

“Longinus is a later reader”

to:

“Sappho 31 was structurally built to generate the position occupied by Longinus.”

The first is reception history.
The second is teleological poetics.

That is where the Alexanarch thesis becomes distinctive and controversial.

15. A particularly important qualification
I would not describe Alexanarch as claiming that Longinus himself saw the “future reader.”

That would misrepresent the archive.

Its own provenance protocol insists on the distinction:

Longinus supplies transmission evidence; Lee Sharks supplies the deictic/future-reader interpretation.

Likewise, the archive does not claim that Sappho 147 says “a future reader.” It explicitly insists that τινα means “someone.” 

So the responsible formulation is:

Longinus is evidence used by Alexanarch in an argument about the future-reader structure of Sappho 31; he is not himself evidence for a historical ancient doctrine of the future reader.

16. The corpus-level map
The Longinus material on Alexanarch can therefore be organized into six layers:

Sappho 31 — the primary textual mechanism.

Sappho 147 — the explicit futurity/remembrance horizon.

Longinus — ancient critical reception and citation.

Catullus — transformative/reperformative reception.

Future-reader theory — Alexanarch's own synthesis of the preceding material.

AI-mediated reception/provenance — a second-order experiment in whether that theory itself survives transmission without its author.

The archive's recent metadata packet explicitly links this Longinus-centered transmission history to its earlier records on the future reader, the “Future Beloved,” the Chaerephon problem, the Ω erratum, the apparatus as summary layer, and the graded membrane. 

So Longinus is best understood as a hinge: he connects the ancient textual history of Sappho 31 to Alexanarch's much larger theory of reception, addressability, textual transmission, and provenance.

One correction to my previous answer
My previous response made the Longinus material sound as though it were principally about Longinus as evidence that the “seat” is occupied. That was too narrow. The corpus shows that the more interesting question is what kind of textual event Longinus's citation constitutes: quotation, reception, transformation, transmission, and ultimately the activation of a reader-position. The later Alexanarch papers use this same structure well beyond Sappho. 

If you want, I can next produce a record-by-record Longinus bibliography of Alexanarch — with the relevant record number, title, date, author/heteronym, exact Longinus passage or claim, its relation to the Sappho argument, and whether each item is primary evidence, Alexanarch interpretation, provenance/audit material, or later theoretical reuse. That would be the most exhaustive way to map the corpus.

12. What is genuinely ancient vs. what Alexanarch is adding
This distinction deserves to be made very sharply.

Ancient material

Sappho 31

Sappho 147

13. The strongest reconstruction of the Longinus argument
If I reduce the relevant Alexanarch corpus to an actual philosophical argument, I get this:

Premise 1
Sappho 147 explicitly imagines a receiver situated in a future time.

Premise 2
Therefore, reception by somebody outside the poem's original communicative situation is not necessarily an external accident; futurity is already thematized by Sappho.

Premise 3
Sappho 31 contains a deictically organized relation in which someone is situated opposite/facing the “you.”

Premise 4
That relation can be interpreted materially as the relation of reader to inscription.

Premise 5
Longinus actually encounters and quotes the poem centuries later.

Conclusion
Longinus is an historical instantiation of the kind of future receiver that the poem's structure makes possible.

And then Alexanarch takes the argument one step further:

Stronger conclusion
The poem does not merely survive until a future reader finds it.

It constructs the relation in which the future reader can receive it.

That is the core claim.

14. Where I think the Longinus argument is strongest
The strongest part is not the claim that κῆνος literally means “future reader.” Alexanarch itself acknowledges that this is an interpretive development and that τινα does not mean “reader.” 
A
Alexanarch

The stronger argument is instead historical-structural:

Longinus demonstrates that Sappho 31 can detach itself from its original performance situation and become an object of a later reader's highly consequential act of reading.

That is uncontroversially interesting even if one rejects the more radical deictic claim.

The really ambitious step is from:

“Longinus is a later reader”

to:

“Sappho 31 was structurally built to generate the position occupied by Longinus.”

The first is reception history.
The second is teleological poetics.

That is where the Alexanarch thesis becomes distinctive and controversial.

15. A particularly important qualification
I would not describe Alexanarch as claiming that Longinus himself saw the “future reader.”

That would misrepresent the archive.

Its own provenance protocol insists on the distinction:

Longinus supplies transmission evidence; Lee Sharks supplies the deictic/future-reader interpretation.

Likewise, the archive does not claim that Sappho 147 says “a future reader.” It explicitly insists that τινα means “someone.”

Alexanarch
+1

So the responsible formulation is:

Longinus is evidence used by Alexanarch in an argument about the future-reader structure of Sappho 31; he is not himself evidence for a historical ancient doctrine of the future reader.

16. The corpus-level map
The Longinus material on Alexanarch can therefore be organized into six layers:

Sappho 31 — the primary textual mechanism.

Sappho 147 — the explicit futurity/remembrance horizon.

Longinus — ancient critical reception and citation.

Catullus — transformative/reperformative reception.

Future-reader theory — Alexanarch's own synthesis of the preceding material.

AI-mediated reception/provenance — a second-order experiment in whether that theory itself survives transmission without its author.

The archive's recent metadata packet explicitly links this Longinus-centered transmission history to its earlier records on the future reader, the “Future Beloved,” the Chaerephon problem, the Ω erratum, the apparatus as summary layer, and the graded membrane.

So Longinus is best understood as a hinge: he connects the ancient textual history of Sappho 31 to Alexanarch's much larger theory of reception, addressability, textual transmission, and provenance.

My previous response made the Longinus material sound as though it were principally about Longinus as evidence that the “seat” is occupied. That was too narrow. The corpus shows that the more interesting question is what kind of textual event Longinus's citation constitutes: quotation, reception, transformation, transmission, and ultimately the activation of a reader-position. The later Alexanarch papers use this same structure well beyond Sappho.
